rv.q: Marcel on the Train is stylish and thoughtful enough to avoid the standard pitfalls
It does provide what the play's harrowing subject demands: a moment of silence.
The show pulls back somewhat from pure physical storytelling as it goes along, which is not a fortunate move because the script is nowhere near as eloquent as the silent Slater.
Slater gives a terrific performance — physically agile and emotionally transparent.
“Marcel on the Train” suggests that Marceau might have partly honed those skills using whatever beauty and light he could summon, trying to escape a cruelty that defies words.
Yet Slater's performance and the chance to see an artist inhabit the artistry of another makes this a trip worth taking.
This thoughtful 100-minute work unfolds as a story all its own.
Certainly, it is a worthwhile reminder that we all have the ability to help our fellow humans.
But “Marcel on the Train,” which Slater co-wrote with its director Marshall Pailet, works better as a showcase than a drama.
Marcel on the Train is everything great theater should be: a profound human story with powerful emotions brought to life by an outstanding cast, director, and design team.
Marcel on the Train is not merely a dramatic theatrical production; it is a haunting and real space: an ever-relevant piece of history transformed into a beautiful memory.
Still, for all its shortcomings, Slater’s fans will definitely want to get aboard this “Train.”
It's realized to a point, though their approach at times leans into broad comedy that misunderstands the sensibilities of its subject.
The script brings to light an important fact about the French Resistance during the Nazi invasion but falls short in developing the character of Marel Marceau.
